Resolving prey taxonomy with WoRMS

Source: vignettes/taxonomy-worms.Rmd
taxonomy-worms.Rmd

DietView can attach a taxonomic lineage to every prey by querying the World Register of Marine Species (WoRMS). This vignette shows how to run the lookup, how to read the log of how each prey was matched, and how to freeze the result so that later runs need no network. The lookup chunks are shown but not run, because they need the worrms package and an internet connection. Everything else runs on the public ICES stomach-content extract that ships with the package (ICES Stomach Content Database, ICES, Copenhagen; extract distributed with the R package stomachr, Lindmark 2026; see ?ices_diet) and on its frozen lineage, ices_lineage.

library(DietView)

# drop non-food items and nematodes (mostly parasites, not prey)
phylum <- ices_lineage$phylum[match(ices_diet$prey_aphia_id, ices_lineage$prey_aphia_id)]
dat <- ices_diet[ices_diet$item_type != "non_food" & !phylum %in% "Nematoda", ]

spec <- dv_spec(
  predator       = "predator_common",
  predator_latin = "predator_latin",
  stomach        = "stomach_id",
  prey_id        = "prey_aphia_id",
  prey_name      = "prey_name",
  weight         = "prey_weight_g",
  count          = "prey_count",
  digestion      = "digestion_label",
  covariates     = c("region", "year", "quarter")
)

Why a lineage, and why unidentified records stay

DietView shows the diet at seven ranks, kingdom to species, by default. Your records rarely carry all seven: identification often stops at a coarse rank. In the ICES data, prey are recorded at every level WoRMS knows:

ids <- unique(stats::na.omit(dat$prey_aphia_id))
sort(table(ices_lineage$worms_rank[ices_lineage$prey_aphia_id %in% ids]), decreasing = TRUE)
#> 
#>           Species            Family             Genus             Class 
#>               110                53                36                13 
#>             Order            Phylum        Infraorder          Subclass 
#>                13                 7                 4                 3 
#>        Parvphylum         Subphylum        Superclass         Gigaclass 
#>                 2                 2                 2                 1 
#>       Infraphylum Phylum (Division)         Subfamily          Suborder 
#>                 1                 1                 1                 1 
#>        Subspecies        Superorder 
#>                 1                 1

Only some of these 252 prey names are species. The others stop at a genus, a family, or something as coarse as “Crustacea” (a subphylum) or “Pisces” (a superclass). DietView never fills in the missing ranks. Below the last rank reached, the record is shown as unidentified at that rank, so every ring of the sunburst still holds all the records and adds up to 100%.

Running the lookup

dv_prepare(taxonomy = "worms") calls dv_taxonomy_worms() once for each distinct prey key, not once per record: here 252 AphiaIDs for 8,530 records. Each record is keyed by its AphiaID when it has one, and by its name otherwise.

prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "worms")
prep

In the ICES data, the only records without an AphiaID are the unidentified material, named “Unidentified material”. That name would be sent to WoRMS as a name, fail the exact match and go to fuzzy matching, which has nothing useful to find. Remove the name from the lookup, so these records stay plainly unidentified (dv_prepare() then warns that they have no key, which is what you want):

lookup <- dat
lookup$prey_name[lookup$item_type == "unidentified"] <- NA
prep <- dv_prepare(lookup, spec, taxonomy = "worms")

How each prey is matched

Each distinct prey gets one row in the log, with a match_type:

match_type Meaning What to do
id The AphiaID is accepted in WoRMS Nothing, unless name_check is "differs"
id_synonym The AphiaID is unaccepted; its accepted ID was used Check that the accepted name is the taxon you meant
id_unchecked WoRMS could not be reached to check the ID Run again later
exact No ID; the name matched exactly Nothing
fuzzy No ID; the name was matched by TAXAMATCH, which tolerates misspellings Check every one: a near match can be a different taxon
unresolved No match Correct the name, or accept that the prey stays unidentified

Matching by AphiaID: id and id_synonym

Every ICES prey record carries an AphiaID, so a lookup on these data runs almost entirely through the first two rows of the table. Most IDs are accepted (id). Some are not. The frozen lineage shows two pairs of names that differ by one letter:

pairs <- c("Aphrodita aculeata", "Aphrodite aculeata",
           "Trisopterus esmarkii", "Trisopterus esmarki")
lin_pairs <- ices_lineage[ices_lineage$scientific_name %in% pairs,
                          c("prey_aphia_id", "scientific_name", "family", "species")]
lin_pairs$n_records <- as.vector(table(dat$prey_aphia_id)[as.character(lin_pairs$prey_aphia_id)])
lin_pairs
#>     prey_aphia_id      scientific_name       family              species
#> 24         126444 Trisopterus esmarkii      Gadidae Trisopterus esmarkii
#> 139        129840   Aphrodita aculeata Aphroditidae   Aphrodita aculeata
#> 310        231869   Aphrodite aculeata Aphroditidae   Aphrodite aculeata
#> 311        400596  Trisopterus esmarki      Gadidae  Trisopterus esmarki
#>     n_records
#> 24         35
#> 139        47
#> 310        31
#> 311        73
table(dat$prey_name[dat$prey_name %in% pairs], dat$country[dat$prey_name %in% pairs])
#>                       
#>                        DE DK NL NO SE
#>   Aphrodita aculeata    8  0 12  0 27
#>   Aphrodite aculeata    0 31  0  0  0
#>   Trisopterus esmarki   0 73  0  0  0
#>   Trisopterus esmarkii  9  0 21  1  4

Each pair is one species (a sea mouse and Norway pout) under two AphiaIDs, and one spelling of each comes from a single country. WoRMS keeps variant spellings like these as unaccepted names with AphiaIDs of their own. A live lookup reads each AphiaID’s record; when it is unaccepted, it follows it to the accepted AphiaID, logs it as id_synonym and gives both spellings the same lineage. The frozen ices_lineage was built from the AphiaIDs as reported, so it keeps them apart, and the species ring counts each species twice. It matters for any species-level statement:

cod <- dat[dat$predator_common == "Atlantic cod", ]
prep_cod <- dv_prepare(cod, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage,
                       verbose = FALSE)
fo <- dv_fo_table(prep_cod, rank = "species")
fo[fo$taxon %in% pairs, ]
#>       rank                taxon n_stomachs n_total pct_fo
#> 5  species   Aphrodita aculeata         42     991   4.24
#> 6  species   Aphrodite aculeata         25     991   2.52
#> 9  species  Trisopterus esmarki         21     991   2.12
#> 14 species Trisopterus esmarkii         15     991   1.51

When you work offline, the same correction is one line per pair, made on your copy of the data before dv_prepare(). Keep it in the script, so the change is visible:

accepted <- c("231869" = 129840L,   # Aphrodite aculeata  -> Aphrodita aculeata
              "400596" = 126444L)   # Trisopterus esmarki -> Trisopterus esmarkii
fix <- as.character(cod$prey_aphia_id) %in% names(accepted)
cod$prey_aphia_id[fix] <- accepted[as.character(cod$prey_aphia_id[fix])]
cod$prey_name[fix] <- ices_lineage$scientific_name[
  match(cod$prey_aphia_id[fix], ices_lineage$prey_aphia_id)]
prep_cod <- dv_prepare(cod, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage,
                       verbose = FALSE)
fo <- dv_fo_table(prep_cod, rank = "species")
fo[fo$taxon %in% pairs, ]
#>      rank                taxon n_stomachs n_total pct_fo
#> 3 species   Aphrodita aculeata         67     991   6.76
#> 6 species Trisopterus esmarkii         36     991   3.63

Merged, the sea mouse is found in 67 cod stomachs (6.76%) and ranks number 2 among the named species of the cod diet by frequency of occurrence; split, its more common spelling ranked number 4.

name_check compares the name in your table with the name WoRMS holds for the AphiaID. In ices_diet the prey names were taken from WoRMS by AphiaID, so they agree by construction. In your own data, "differs" usually means that a name or an ID was mistyped, and the two point to different taxa.

Matching by name: exact and fuzzy

Names are used only when there is no AphiaID. To see what that path does, take a few ICES prey names, one of them misspelled:

keys <- data.frame(prey_id   = NA,
                   prey_name = c("Crangon crangon", "Ammodytidae", "Crangon crangom"))
dv_taxonomy_worms(keys)

The first two names should come back as exact. The third fails the exact match; with fuzzy = TRUE, WoRMS TAXAMATCH proposes the closest name it knows and the row is logged as fuzzy, with the proposal in matched_name. For a one-letter slip the proposal is usually the intended name, but a near match can just as well be another taxon one letter away. Check every fuzzy row.

The other columns of the log

lineage_ok is FALSE when the prey was matched but WoRMS returned no classification, for example because the connection failed. Those prey count as unidentified at every rank until you run the lookup again. Failed lookups are not stored in the cache, so the next run asks WoRMS again. names_seen lists every name found under one key: more than one name under the same AphiaID is worth a look. homonym flags a name with several accepted WoRMS records.

Successful lookups are cached on disk (in tools::R_user_dir("DietView", "cache")), so a rerun only queries what changed. The log also records when the taxonomy was retrieved and which worrms version was used, in its retrieved and worrms_version attributes.

Reading the report

dv_taxonomy_report() returns the prey that need a look, largest number of records first:

review <- dv_taxonomy_report(prep, which = "review")
review

# the whole log, to archive or to send to a co-author
dv_taxonomy_report(prep, which = "all", file = file.path(tempdir(), "taxonomy_log.csv"))

On the ICES data, the rows to expect there are unaccepted AphiaIDs (id_synonym), with the number of records each one affects. Unresolved prey you did not expect are the ones to chase.

The frozen alternative: ices_lineage

A lineage table is the reproducible path: no network, no change between runs. ices_lineage is one such table, with one row per AphiaID:

dim(ices_lineage)
#> [1] 461  10
ices_lineage[ices_lineage$scientific_name %in% c("Crangon crangon", "Ammodytidae",
                                                  "Crustacea", "Pisces"), ]
#>    prey_aphia_id scientific_name worms_rank  kingdom     phylum        class
#> 48        107552 Crangon crangon    Species Animalia Arthropoda Malacostraca
#> 77          1066       Crustacea  Subphylum Animalia Arthropoda         <NA>
#> 81         11676          Pisces Superclass Animalia   Chordata         <NA>
#> 92        125516     Ammodytidae     Family Animalia   Chordata    Teleostei
#>          order      family   genus         species
#> 48    Decapoda Crangonidae Crangon Crangon crangon
#> 77        <NA>        <NA>    <NA>            <NA>
#> 81        <NA>        <NA>    <NA>            <NA>
#> 92 Perciformes Ammodytidae    <NA>            <NA>

It was not produced by dv_taxonomy_worms(). It comes from the WoRMS classification that the R package stomachr (Lindmark 2026) compiled for the AphiaIDs of the ICES extract; the script data-raw/ices_data.R in the package sources reshapes it into DietView’s seven ranks. Two columns are derived there rather than read from WoRMS: kingdom, from the phylum, and species, from the name when its WoRMS rank is species or subspecies (a subspecies is reported under its species). A name above species keeps only the ranks WoRMS gives it, so “Crustacea” has a phylum and nothing below. It is used with taxonomy = "table"; the key column prey_aphia_id has the same name as the prey key of ices_diet:

prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage,
                   verbose = FALSE)
prep
#> <dietview_prep>
#>   records   : 8530 
#>   stomachs  : 4222 
#>   predators : 22 
#>   ranks     : kingdom > phylum > class > order > family > genus > species 
#>   covariates: region, year, quarter 
#>   source    : table

A table path has no match log: the lineage is taken as given. dv_prepare() warns if a prey key is missing from the table, and those records are kept as unidentified at every rank.

Correcting and freezing your own lookup

Fix the names or IDs the report lists in your source table and run the lookup again. When the log is clean, save the lineage, keyed by the same column as your data, and switch to the offline path for every later run:

lineage <- unique(prep$data[, c(spec$prey_id, prep$ranks)])
lin_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "lineage_2026-10-20.csv")   # use your project folder
write.csv(lineage, lin_file, row.names = FALSE)

lineage <- read.csv(lin_file, na.strings = c("NA", ""))
prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = lineage)

The lineage table fixes the taxonomic snapshot your figures were made from. Archive it with your data, together with the log, and note the retrieval date and the worrms version, because WoRMS changes.

Exact matching only

To turn off TAXAMATCH matching and keep only known AphiaIDs and exact names:

prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "worms", fuzzy = FALSE)
